title: Demonstrate a basic understanding of the physiological functioning of the anatomical structures of the plant

lessons.title: Roots, stems and transport tissues
lessons.html:
Structure and function

Plant anatomy is the internal structure of plants; physiology is how those structures work. Understanding both helps you see why practices such as irrigation, pruning and fertilising affect crops.

Roots

  • Root cap: protects the growing tip as it pushes through soil.
  • Growing zone: just behind the tip, where cells divide and lengthen.
  • Root hairs: tiny extensions of outer cells that vastly increase surface area for absorbing water and nutrients. They are easily damaged during transplanting, which is why transplants wilt.
  • Taproots (e.g. carrots, lucerne) go deep; fibrous roots (e.g. maize, grasses) spread near the surface.

Roots need oxygen to respire. In waterlogged or compacted soil, roots suffocate and stop absorbing water, so plants may wilt even in wet soil.

Many roots form partnerships: legumes such as beans, soybeans and lucerne host Rhizobium bacteria in root nodules that fix nitrogen from the air. Mycorrhizal fungi extend the root system and help take up phosphorus.

Stems

The stem supports leaves and flowers and contains the transport system:

  • Xylem: carries water and dissolved minerals upward from the roots. In woody plants, xylem forms the wood.
  • Phloem: carries sugars made in the leaves to where they are needed: roots, fruit, growing tips and storage organs. It lies just under the bark.
  • Cambium: a layer of dividing cells between xylem and phloem that makes the stem thicker each year.

Because phloem lies just under the bark, damaging the bark all the way around a tree (ring-barking by animals or careless tools) stops sugar reaching the roots and can kill the tree. Grafting works because the cambium of scion and rootstock grow together.

Buds and meristems

Meristems are zones of active cell division at shoot and root tips and in buds. The tip bud often suppresses side buds (apical dominance); removing the tip, as in topping or pinching, encourages side shoots.

lessons.title: Leaves, flowers, fruit and seeds
lessons.html:
Leaves: the food factory

Leaf structure is built for photosynthesis and gas exchange.

  • Cuticle: a waxy layer that reduces water loss. Thick in drought-adapted plants like aloes.
  • Mesophyll: cells full of chloroplasts, where photosynthesis happens: carbon dioxide plus water, using light energy, produces sugar and releases oxygen.
  • Veins: xylem and phloem bundles that supply water and carry sugars away.
  • Stomata: tiny pores, mostly on the underside, opened and closed by guard cells. They let carbon dioxide in and water vapour out (transpiration).

Transpiration pulls water up the xylem from the roots and cools the leaf. On hot, dry, windy days plants close stomata to save water, which also slows photosynthesis and growth. This is why water stress reduces yield even before wilting is visible.

Respiration

All living cells respire, using sugars and oxygen to release energy, day and night. Harvested fruit and vegetables keep respiring, which is why cooling them slows deterioration.

Flowers

  • Sepals and petals: protect the bud and attract pollinators.
  • Stamens (anther and filament): produce pollen.
  • Pistil (stigma, style, ovary): receives pollen; the ovary contains ovules.

Pollination moves pollen to the stigma by wind (maize, wheat), insects (most fruit trees, pumpkins) or birds. Fertilisation follows, and ovules become seeds while the ovary becomes the fruit. Poor pollination gives misshapen or small fruit, which is why orchards hire beehives during bloom.

Fruit and seeds

Fruit protects seeds and helps spread them. A seed contains an embryo, stored food (endosperm or cotyledons) and a seed coat. Monocots such as maize have one seed leaf; dicots such as beans have two.

Storage organs

Tubers (potato), bulbs (onion), tuberous roots (sweet potato) and taproots (carrot) store sugars and starch made in leaves. Healthy leaves are therefore essential for big storage organs.

Key points

  • Root hairs absorb water and nutrients and need oxygen.
  • Xylem carries water up; phloem carries sugars from leaves.
  • Leaves photosynthesise; stomata control gas exchange and transpiration.
  • Flowers produce seeds after pollination; the ovary becomes the fruit.
  • Harvested produce keeps respiring, so cooling extends shelf life.
